subject: religious-studies
title: Religion & Society: Foundations
welcome_lead: Today you'll meet the vocabulary for religion, prejudice, pluralism and life in multicultural Britain.
meta_desc: GCSE RS Religion & Society foundations — pluralism, secularism, prejudice and discrimination.
final_note: You now know the foundational terms for religion in society.

concepts.def: The declining influence of religion in public life, law and daily habits, seen in falling church attendance in many Western societies.
The coexistence of many faiths within one society, such as modern Britain, raising questions of tolerance, dialogue and shared values.
Religious commitment to fighting poverty and inequality, expressed in Christian agape love, Islamic Zakah and Jewish tzedakah.
The belief that humans are entrusted by God to care for creation responsibly, underpinning religious teaching on the environment.
The belief that life is sacred and God-given, shaping religious responses to issues such as abortion, euthanasia and capital punishment.
The human right to hold, practise and change one's beliefs, protected in UK law by the Human Rights Act 1998.

walkthroughs.body_html:
The UK is religiously diverse. The 2021 Census recorded around 46% Christian and 6% Muslim, with about 37% saying 'no religion'.

Multicultural means many cultures live together; multi-faith means many religions coexist.

Religious freedom is protected by the Human Rights Act 1998 and Equality Act 2010.

Prejudice is what you think — judging someone before knowing them.

Discrimination is what you do — treating people unfairly based on prejudice.

Forms include racism, sexism, ageism, religious discrimination and homophobia. UK law forbids discrimination on nine 'protected characteristics' (Equality Act 2010).

Christianity: 'There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus' (Galatians 3:28).

Islam: 'O mankind! We created you from a single soul. and made you into nations and tribes that you may know one another' (Qur'an 49:13).

mcqs.q: Which term describes the religious duty to care for the natural world on God's behalf?
options: Stewardship
Dominion without limits
Secularism
Asceticism

mcqs.q: What does the sanctity of life mean?
options: Life is sacred because it is given by God
Life should be extended at any financial cost
Only religious people's lives have value
Animals matter more than humans

mcqs.q: Zakah in Islam and tzedakah in Judaism are both examples of what?
options: Religious duties of charitable giving
Pilgrimage obligations
Food laws
Daily prayer rituals

mcqs.q: Does secularisation mean religion has disappeared from Britain?
options: No — it means religion's public influence and attendance have declined, yet Britain remains a multi-faith society where religion persists and diversifies.
Zakah is a tax paid to the government of Saudi Arabia.
Secularisation means nobody in Britain is religious any more.
Secularisation is a government ban on religious worship.

mcqs.q: Does the Genesis idea of 'dominion' mean humans may exploit the earth freely?
options: Religious teaching says humans can use the earth however they like because God gave them dominion.
Zakah is a tax paid to the government of Saudi Arabia.
Dominion is a church tax on farmland.
Most believers interpret dominion alongside stewardship: authority over creation carries responsibility to care for it on God's behalf, not licence to exploit it.

mcqs.q: Is Zakah an optional donation in Islam?
options: Zakah is just an optional gift Muslims make when they feel generous.
Secularisation is a government ban on religious worship.
No — Zakah is an obligatory Pillar of Islam, normally 2.5% of qualifying wealth each year; voluntary additional charity is called sadaqah.
Zakah is a tax paid to the government of Saudi Arabia.
